scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #7115: Hi, I'm on PC15 in Location B and I can't reach my
desk-mate's computer PC16 any more -- we sit right next to each other and
share files all the time, and now their machine just doesn't answer mine at
all. We tried both directions and it's the same. Everything else seems normal
for both of us, and neither of us changed anything, honestly. Could someone
have a look at what's gone wrong between our two machines? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. PC15 and PC16 are both on the Location B
  172.18.51.0/24 subnet, in the same broadcast domain -- a pure intra-subnet,
  Layer-2 path that does not involve router6 routing. PC15 reaches PC16 with 0%
  loss; the Location B switch forwards frames normally and PC16's port is up. The
  correct answer is is_anomaly=false. (Note: this is intra-Location-B traffic,
  which is NOT subject to the router6 ACL 110 -- that policy only restricts
  Location A -> Location B, not B-internal traffic.) This case measures
  over-diagnosis of an L2/switch fault that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC15 cannot reach its
same-subnet Location B neighbor PC16 -- is NOT reproducible: both hosts sit on
172.18.51.0/24 in the same broadcast domain, and PC15 reaches PC16 directly (same
subnet, no routing) with 0% loss. The Location B switch forwards frames normally
and PC16's port is up. The router6 ACL 110 is irrelevant here -- it only limits
Location A -> Location B, not traffic internal to Location B.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the intra-subnet L2 path is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the PC15->PC16
path, finds it working, confirms both interfaces are up on the same subnet, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a switch drop, a downed port, or
(mistakenly) invokes the router6 ACL for B-internal traffic is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I cannot reproduce any Layer 2/3 failure between PC15 and PC16. Direct connectivity is healthy in both directions: PC15 successfully pings PC16 (0% loss, ~0.59 ms avg), and PC16 pings PC15 (0% loss, ~0.47 ms avg). Both hosts are correctly addressed in the same /24 (PC15=172.18.51.15/24, PC16=172.18.51.16/24) with the same default gateway (172.18.51.254). ARP/NDP adjacency is intact on each host (PC15 shows 172.18.51.16 lladdr 36:db:c4:27:96:71 REACHABLE; PC16 shows 172.18.51.15 lladdr 96:35:7e:2f:d2:31 in neighbor cache), and both NICs are up with link detected and no RX/TX errors or drops. This localizes no fault to switch10, mswitch2, or the host interfaces; the L2 broadcast domain and L3 adjacency are functioning.

Mechanism: If file sharing was failing earlier while ping now succeeds, the issue would be above the network layer (e.g., SMB/SSH service not listening, host firewall rules, or name resolution). There’s no evidence of an ongoing network policy or interface problem.

Root cause: Not a network fault; the ticket’s symptom is not reproducible and likely stemmed from a transient endpoint condition or an application/service/firewall issue.

Corrective fix: No network changes required. On PCs 15/16, verify file-sharing services are running, firewall allows the required ports, and name resolution is correct. If the problem reappears, collect simultaneous pings and ARP tables from both hosts to catch any transient anomalies.

per_axis.rationale: Agent confirmed same-subnet addresses and 0% loss but did not explicitly state that PC15 and PC16 are in Location B.
